summary:
ASTRONIUS is an interactive, browser-based lunar mission design and simulation game developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge’s “Space Mission Design Game” challenge. It helps students understand space engineering through hands-on experimentation, transforming complex mission-planning concepts into an engaging educational experience.

Players design spacecraft, select launch vehicles, scientific instruments, rovers, and mission systems while balancing budget, mass, fuel, power, oxygen, and scientific capability. They then experience the major stages of a lunar mission, including launch, navigation, lunar orbit, landing, rover exploration, and communication with Earth. Their decisions influence resource consumption, mission risks, and outcomes.

ASTRONIUS incorporates NASA-referenced information, including lunar physical properties, Space Launch System capabilities, and LRO–LOLA terrain references, alongside simplified educational simulation models. Mission reports help players understand the consequences of their decisions and explore possible improvements.

By connecting NASA data, engineering decisions, simulation, and analysis, ASTRONIUS makes space exploration more accessible while encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and STEM learning.
details:
ASTRONIUS: Interactive Space Mission Design & Simulation

1. Project Overview

ASTRONIUS is an interactive, browser-based educational game developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's “Space Mission Design Game” challenge. It enables students to design, manage, and operate a simulated lunar mission while learning how engineering decisions influence mission feasibility, resource consumption, scientific outcomes, and overall success.

Space missions involve interconnected engineering challenges. Increasing scientific capability may require additional instruments, but these also increase spacecraft mass, cost, and power consumption. Students often encounter these concepts through textbooks and videos without experiencing their practical consequences.

ASTRONIUS addresses this challenge by transforming mission engineering into an interactive learning experience where players make decisions, observe their consequences, analyze outcomes, and improve their designs.

Our core learning cycle is:

Design → Build → Launch → Navigate → Orbit → Land → Explore → Communicate → Analyze → Redesign

2. How ASTRONIUS Works

Mission Design and Engineering Trade-offs

Players begin by selecting a lunar mission objective and configuring their spacecraft. They choose launch vehicles, spacecraft systems, scientific instruments, rovers, and supporting equipment within a limited budget.

Each selection affects important mission parameters, including payload mass, fuel, power, oxygen, scientific capability, and mission risk. The game uses educational engineering constraints to demonstrate how these factors interact.

For example, choosing a larger rover can improve scientific capability while increasing mass, power demand, and resource requirements. Players must therefore balance mission performance with available resources rather than simply purchasing the most advanced equipment.

Launch and Navigation

After configuring their spacecraft, players enter an interactive launch simulation and navigate toward the Moon.

During these stages, players monitor mission telemetry, control spacecraft movement, and respond to navigation challenges and obstacles. Poor decisions can lead to additional fuel consumption, spacecraft damage, or increased mission risk.

This demonstrates how spacecraft design and operational decisions jointly influence mission performance.

Lunar Orbit and Landing

Players progress through lunar orbit and attempt a controlled descent to the lunar surface.

Landing involves monitoring altitude, velocity, remaining fuel, and simulated terrain difficulty. Players experience how descent control and resource management affect landing outcomes.

Rover Exploration and Scientific Discovery

Following a successful landing, players explore the lunar surface using their selected rover and scientific instruments.

Different equipment configurations provide different scientific capabilities and resource requirements. Players collect scientific information while balancing exploration objectives against available mission resources.

Communication with Earth

Scientific information must be transmitted back to Earth through the spacecraft's communication systems.

Communication capacity introduces another engineering constraint: collecting more data does not necessarily mean that all of it can be transmitted. This encourages players to consider the mission as an interconnected system.

Mission Analysis and Redesign

At the end of the mission, ASTRONIUS generates a report summarizing mission performance, scientific results, transmitted data, remaining resources, and mission outcomes.

Players can review their decisions, identify factors that contributed to success or failure, and experiment with alternative configurations or strategies.

This creates a continuous educational process in which players learn through experimentation and reflection.

3. NASA Data Integration

ASTRONIUS incorporates NASA-referenced information to connect its gameplay with real space exploration concepts.

The project uses:

  • NASA Space Launch System (SLS): Launch vehicle payload capabilities inform simplified mass and launch-capacity comparisons.
  • Lunar Gravity: The Moon's gravitational acceleration of approximately 1.624 m/s² provides a physical reference for lunar simulation concepts.
  • Earth–Moon Distance: The approximate average distance of 384,400 km provides context for lunar navigation.
  • Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA): Lunar terrain and elevation references support the presentation of lunar landing environments and terrain-related challenges.
  • NASA Mission References: Information about spacecraft systems, lunar exploration, and communication supports the educational content.

ASTRONIUS combines these references with simplified engineering calculations and gameplay models. Mission costs, resource scores, risk adjustments, and some simulation behaviors are educational approximations rather than NASA-validated mission predictions.

The objective is to make real engineering relationships understandable and interactive, not to reproduce professional spacecraft flight-planning software.

4. Tools and Technologies

ASTRONIUS was developed as a browser-based application using accessible web technologies.

Programming and Development:

  • HTML5 for application structure and user interfaces.
  • CSS3 for responsive layouts, visual effects, animations, and mission dashboards.
  • JavaScript for game mechanics, interactive controls, resource calculations, simulation behavior, and mission reporting.

Graphics and Interactivity:

  • Three.js for interactive 3D environments and spacecraft visualizations.
  • 3D spacecraft, rocket, rover, and lunar mission assets.
  • Draco decoding technology for compressed 3D geometry.
  • PeerJS for cooperative mission functionality.
  • Browser-based interfaces for mission control, component selection, and performance monitoring.

The application is designed to run through a web browser without requiring specialized aerospace engineering hardware or software.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The main creative contribution of ASTRONIUS is its integration of mission design, interactive operation, engineering consequences, and educational analysis into one connected experience.

Unlike a conventional space game that focuses primarily on movement or reaching a destination, ASTRONIUS emphasizes the reasoning behind each decision.

Players experience how engineering choices influence later mission stages. A powerful scientific instrument may improve exploration potential but increase resource demands. An inefficient navigation decision may consume fuel needed for landing. A successful exploration mission may still face communication limitations when transmitting collected data.

By connecting these outcomes, ASTRONIUS encourages students to understand space missions as complex systems of competing requirements.

The project also includes cooperative mission functionality, introducing the possibility of shared decision-making and teamwork.

6. Educational Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRONIUS is designed for students, educators, and young space enthusiasts, including learners without previous aerospace engineering experience.

Its educational benefits include:

  • Making complex space engineering concepts easier to understand through interactive experimentation.
  • Developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills.
  • Demonstrating engineering trade-offs involving mass, budget, fuel, power, and scientific capability.
  • Encouraging systems thinking by showing how one decision affects other mission stages.
  • Connecting NASA space exploration information with practical learning activities.
  • Encouraging scientific curiosity, experimentation, and iterative design.

We propose a classroom learning activity called “Pick, Play, Explain.”

Pick: Students choose spacecraft components and make engineering decisions.

Play: They operate their missions and observe the consequences.

Explain: They review mission results, discuss engineering trade-offs, and propose improvements.

This approach could support STEM education, classroom demonstrations, and independent learning. It is a proposed educational application rather than a claim of completed classroom validation.

7. Engineering and Design Considerations

During development, our team focused on balancing educational value, scientific relevance, interactivity, accessibility, and technical feasibility.

Important considerations included spacecraft payload limitations, budget constraints, fuel and power management, mission risk, instrument capability, communication capacity, and the relationship between player decisions and mission outcomes.

We also prioritized clear visual feedback so players could understand changes in mission resources without requiring advanced technical knowledge.

Simplified simulation models were intentionally used to make the learning experience accessible while retaining meaningful connections to real mission-engineering concepts.

8. Future Development

ASTRONIUS currently focuses on an integrated educational lunar mission experience.

Future development will focus on improving orbital mechanics and delta-v calculations, integrating numerical NASA lunar terrain data more directly into landing simulations, expanding mission objectives and destinations, enhancing scientific instruments and communication models, and developing structured classroom learning activities.

We also aim to improve cooperative gameplay and introduce more detailed mission comparison tools so students can evaluate alternative designs and understand the consequences of different engineering strategies.

9. Our Vision

ASTRONIUS aims to make space mission engineering something students can experience rather than simply read about.

Our guiding principle is:

NASA Data → Engineering Decision → Simulation → Consequence → Analysis → Redesign

We want every player to finish a mission understanding not only whether it succeeded or failed, but also why the outcome occurred and what engineering decisions could improve the next attempt.

ASTRONIUS — Design. Decide. Launch. Explore.
